Virginia Beach at a glance

With 459,470 people counted in 2020 and 453,737 estimated for 2025, Virginia Beach ranks first among Virginia's cities. The Atlantic lies to the east and the Chesapeake Bay to the north. Norfolk is 19 miles west. About 245 square miles are land, another 253 are water, and the typical elevation is only 12 feet.

The Green Line, an urban growth boundary, splits the built-up north from the farmland and open country in the south. Vacant ground north of the line is running short, which keeps resale and redevelopment busy.

Today's city came from a 1963 merger of Princess Anne County with the small resort city. Seven boroughs resulted: Bayside, Blackwater, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Princess Anne, Pungo and Virginia Beach. An address here might be a beachfront block, a cul-de-sac subdivision or a working farm. Name the neighborhood when you talk with a buyer. Sandbridge, Thalia, Great Neck Point, Oceana and Green Run attract very different shoppers, and a short drive changes the audience.

Flooding and a Virginia Beach sale

Low ground and a lot of surrounding water make flooding the main environmental worry for many homes. Hurricane Matthew's rain put more than 2,000 houses under water, and a few neighborhoods stayed flooded for days. The city then rejected several floodplain building proposals, and when developers sued, they lost.

Buyers remember that. Expect inspectors and insurance agents to probe. A short prep list helps:

  • Call your insurer to learn whether the parcel requires flood coverage, and at what premium.
  • Pull together elevation certificates, repair receipts and past claims.
  • Disclose earlier water in the house to a cash buyer up front. A direct purchaser can lower the price for the damage instead of walking away after the inspection.

Water damage, postponed repairs or a tenant still in the unit are all reasons a cash purchase as is can beat months of fix-ups and open houses.

Selling on a military timeline

The economy leans on bases, visitors and corporate offices. NAS Oceana employs more people than anyone else in the city. Joint Expeditionary Base East at Cape Henry, Training Support Center Hampton Roads and Naval Amphibious Base Little Creek are either inside the city or next door.

Service members with orders often face a fixed moving date, and certainty is worth more than a slightly higher price. A buyer who does not depend on a lender's underwriting can usually name a closing day and hold to it. Share your date at the outset, and ask the buyer what paperwork is needed on your end.

Visitor traffic also supports hotels, restaurants and short-term rentals near the oceanfront. An owner of a vacation or investment property may want out after a slow season.

  • Deeds recorded at the Circuit Court clerk's office update the ownership records kept by the Real Estate Assessor.

Taxes and fees at closing

Taxes for the current year are split by the day. The full annual amount for the fiscal year is the base, and the installment dates do not create separate periods. The closing agent runs the math and shows it on your settlement sheet.

Deed taxes are separate from the property tax. Virginia charges 25 cents per $100 for recordation under section 58.1-801. The grantor tax falls on the seller at 50 cents per $500 under section 58.1-802, though a buyer may agree to absorb it.

Page one of the deed has to show the price before the clerk will record it. Also settle any overdue balance beforehand. The Treasurer applies delinquent amounts first and only then releases a refund. Request a payoff number as your closing nears.

Inherited, estate and trust sales

Under section 55.1-702, the Residential Property Disclosure Act does not reach every kind of transfer. A fiduciary handling an estate, guardianship, conservatorship or trust is excluded, as are transfers after foreclosure and transfers between spouses or to lineal relatives.

Whether your transaction fits one of those boxes turns on its facts, so a short call with a probate lawyer is worthwhile.

Heirs should line up three documents before talking to buyers: a death certificate, the court order naming whoever may sign for the estate, and the most recent tax bill. Title companies and purchasers ask for these first.

No lender is involved, so nothing depends on a buyer's loan being approved. That matters most when flood damage, overdue repairs, tenants or a transfer to another duty station would make an ordinary listing slow or shaky.

  • A title search turns up liens, unpaid taxes and other items that need clearing.
  • Your proceeds pay off taxes and any mortgage at closing, and every payoff appears as a separate line.
  • After the grantor tax is paid and the price is on the first page, the deed goes on record with the Circuit Court clerk.

Nothing obliges you to say yes. Take the figure home and run your own numbers first.

What to gather before you talk to a buyer

A little preparation shortens the whole process. Keep these in one folder, on paper or on your phone:

  • Your latest real estate tax bill, plus proof of which installments you have paid.
  • The most recent mortgage statement, if a loan is still open, so a payoff can be requested.
  • Flood paperwork: elevation certificates, insurance claims and repair records.
  • A note on which community or borough the house is in, and anything unusual about the lot.

With those in hand, a buyer can make a firm offer faster, and your closing agent can order the title work without waiting on you.

Getting around the city

Commute questions come up on every showing. Norfolk International Airport runs along the line shared with Norfolk. Atlantic Avenue has Hampton Roads Transit bus service, and Amtrak stops at Norfolk and Newport News with bus connections. The Greyhound terminal is on Laskin Road, roughly a mile west of the oceanfront.

Know the parking situation and the drive to the base or the beach, because buyers will ask.

Bills come in two installments, on December 5 and June 5. A weekend or holiday due date slides to the next business day.

They are figured by the day from the full annual tax for the fiscal year. Your closing agent puts the split on the settlement sheet.

Yes. Plenty of buyers avoid flood damage, but a direct cash buyer can subtract the repair cost and purchase as is. Collect any insurance claims and repair records first.

Seven: Bayside, Blackwater, Kempsville, Lynnhaven, Princess Anne, Pungo and Virginia Beach. They come from the 1963 merger of Princess Anne County and the city.

Chesapeake at a glance

Land area makes Chesapeake the second largest city in Virginia: about 351 square miles in all, with roughly 338 of them dry. Neighborhoods near Norfolk are dense, while roads out by the North Carolina line run past farms and woods. The Census Bureau put the 2020 population at 249,422 and the 2025 estimate at 255,332.

The city also holds a slice of the Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge, and much more acreage is protected farmland, forest or wetland. A 1963 merger of South Norfolk with the rest of Norfolk County produced Chesapeake, so it never grew a single downtown. Instead you get named communities such as Great Bridge, Deep Creek, Western Branch, Butts Road, Pleasant Grove, Washington and South Norfolk.

This matters when you set an asking price. Someone shopping in Great Bridge may know little about Deep Creek, and a house built in one decade can have very different wiring, lot size and repair history from one built in another.

Water, drainage and flood risk

Sitting about 16 feet above sea level among tidal rivers, canals and swamp, Chesapeake houses deal with water more than most. July highs average near 88 degrees and January highs near 50, with about 48 inches of precipitation in an ordinary year.

Soggy crawl spaces, poor grading and lots that flood after hard rain are what keep a listed house on the market. Appraisers and buyers' inspectors go looking for them first.

  • Crawl space: standing water, soft floor framing, a vapor barrier that has failed.
  • Outside: gutters, the slope of the yard, and any sump pump or French drain added later.
  • Insurance: find out the flood zone before pricing, because a financed buyer has to insure the house.
  • Roof: humid summers and storm winds wear shingles out sooner than owners expect.

The city treats water from the Northwest River with reverse osmosis, since that river turns salty at times, and the wider region also gets supply through a 76-mile pipeline from Lake Gaston.

Getting around the city

Drive time comes up in almost every buyer conversation. Interstate 64 is part of the Hampton Roads Beltway, I-464 heads to Norfolk and Portsmouth, and I-664 heads to Newport News. U.S. 13, 17, 58 and 460 cross the city, and State Route 168 includes the Chesapeake Expressway toll road.

The city keeps up 90 bridges and overpasses, five of them drawbridges that lift an estimated 30,000 times a year. Sitting through an opening at rush hour changes how an address feels, so some buyers weigh it. Hampton Roads Transit runs the buses, and Norfolk International is the closest commercial airport.

Northwest Annex and Naval Auxiliary Landing Field Fentress, both Navy sites, are inside the city. Orders, retirement or a relative's estate can force a sale on someone else's calendar.

Selling with taxes owed

Back taxes on a Virginia parcel become a lien that jumps the queue ahead of most other claims, and it stays on the property until the city is paid. How the current year's bill gets divided between you and the buyer is spelled out in the sales contract.

  • Title search: ask for liens, judgments and utility bills left unpaid.
  • Estates: confirm which heir or executor has authority to sign.

The trouble is usually the house, not the market: water damage on low ground, long-deferred repairs in older South Norfolk and Deep Creek homes, or a tenant who is hard to move.

  • An empty inherited house still collecting tax and insurance bills.
  • Moisture, mold or rot that blocks conventional loan approval.
  • A military or civilian transfer with a short fuse.
  • A rental where the tenant stays put or the lease has lapsed.

A cash buyer takes the house as is, so there are no contractors to schedule and no strangers walking through on your weekends. Sometimes we purchase directly and sometimes a vetted cash buyer does; the offer tells you which.

From offer to closing

Send the address, condition, occupancy and any known debts, and we write an offer. Accept, and a local title company starts searching for liens, judgments and back taxes.

No bank is underwriting, so the title search sets the pace. Count on weeks rather than months, longer if a lien or an open estate complicates things. You name the closing day within that window and sign at the title office, or by mail when you live out of town.

Round up the deed, the latest tax bill and, for an estate, whatever shows who may sign. Owners who moved away, military families among them, can close using signed documents and a local title company.

Weighing a cash offer against listing

Listing makes sense if the house is in decent shape and you can wait. You will field showings and inspection requests, and the buyer may still need a loan. Cash trades some price for speed and a closing day that sticks.

Compare by totaling the cost of listing: fixing a damp crawl space or tired roof, the agent's fee, and every month of taxes, insurance and utilities while it sits. Take that off the listing price and hold the remainder against the cash figure. Whoever makes the offer should put it in writing and name who pays for title work.

Low ground deserves a thought. A wet crawl space or a street that floods can draw an appraiser's flag, and a flagged house sometimes falls out of a financed deal late. Cash sidesteps the appraisal, but the price will reflect the condition.

How fast can I sell my house in Chesapeake for cash?

It depends on title and the closing date you choose. A cash sale has no lender underwriting, so the title company's pace sets the schedule. If liens or estate paperwork are involved, allow more time.

The four installments fall on September 30, December 31, March 31 and June 5. Confirm the amount with the Treasurer's office before closing, because any unpaid balance is paid from the sale proceeds.

Does Virginia charge a tax when I sell a house?

Yes. The grantor tax is 50 cents per $500 of the sale price, and the seller normally pays it unless the contract says otherwise. Your title company will show the exact amount on the settlement statement.

Can I sell a Chesapeake house that is in a flood zone or has water damage?

Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a house with moisture problems or a weak crawl space, and the offer reflects the repairs. A flood zone matters more to a financed buyer's insurance than to a cash buyer.

The City Real Estate Assessor, at 757-382-6235, can walk you through how your land and buildings were valued at 100 percent of market value.

Richmond, the state capital, answers to no county. It gained independent-city status in 1871 after incorporating in 1742. The 2025 estimate is 237,257 residents, up from 226,610 in the 2020 census, which makes Richmond the fourth most populous city in the state.

People here describe the city in four parts: the North Side, Southside, East End and West End. Housing runs from Victorian townhouses to mid-century ranches, so the story of a house depends a lot on which side of the James River it stands.

How Richmond grew, and why it matters for older houses

The first street grid dates to 1737 and covered the land between today's Broad, 17th and 25th streets and the river. Downtown now sits a little west of that, on the slopes of Shockoe Hill. Many North Side districts were built up after the streetcar arrived and are now listed historic districts.

Southside has its own story. Richmond absorbed the former city of Manchester in 1910. On January 1, 1970, the city grew south by 27 square miles and picked up 47,000 residents, after Chesterfield County lost a court fight against the annexation. Flooding on the James

The James River reaches tidewater at Richmond, and flooding can happen in any month, most often in March and least often in July. Hurricanes and tropical storms have caused most summer and early fall floods. Three hurricanes in 1955, Connie and Diane among them, brought record rainfall over six weeks. In 2004 the remnants of Hurricane Gaston dropped up to 12 inches of rain and did extensive damage downtown.

A flood wall finished in 1995 protects the low-lying parts of the city. Shockoe Bottom, the low ground between Shockoe Hill and Church Hill, is the area most tied to river flooding.

  • Find out whether your lot sits in a mapped floodplain before you list.
  • Check the basement or lowest floor for stains, mold or a sump pump that no longer runs.
  • Pull together insurance and repair records for past water damage.

Winter weather and vacant houses

Winters are moderately cold and summers hot and humid. Snow averages 10.5 inches a season, though it rarely lingers more than a day or two, and ice storms are common but seldom severe. The real risk is an empty house during a cold snap. In an unheated house, one leaky pipe can become a big repair bill, and old roofs and gutters suffer as well.

With an inherited house you are not using, keep the heat on low or shut off the water, and ask someone to check in. Selling ends that worry.

Law, finance and government drive the economy. Downtown holds federal, state and local agencies plus large law and banking firms, and the metro area is home to several Fortune 500 companies. Virginia Commonwealth University and its Medical College of Virginia campus anchor the Virginia BioTechnology Research Park, which opened in 1995.

Roads and commutes

Downtown has long been a hub for boats at the Great Turning Basin, for rail, and for two major interstates that cross. Interstates 95, 64 and 195 all touch the city's neighborhoods. The city is about 21 miles north of Petersburg and sits inside the larger Richmond-Petersburg metro area with Chesterfield, Henrico and Hanover counties.

When you describe your house, mention the nearest interstate access, which side of the river it is on and how far it is from VCU or downtown. Buyers weigh those details heavily.

Sale price triggers a state grantor tax of 50 cents per $500, owed by the seller unless the buyer agrees to take it on. No deed is recorded until the clerk certifies the tax, and the state and the locality divide it evenly. Read the law at Virginia Code 58.1-802.

Pack a photo ID, your deed if you hold a copy, and mortgage account details if a loan remains. Landlords add the leases and tenant contacts, while heirs add proof of who can sign for the estate. Choosing between a listing and a direct sale

Listing the usual way involves prep work, showings, repair talks after the inspection and a wait on the buyer's bank. Selling directly skips nearly all of it. Listing tends to suit a house in good shape when you can wait for the best price. A direct sale suits a house with damage, tenants, a probate calendar or a deadline. Whichever way you lean, compare what you would actually receive after taxes, repairs and holding costs, not just the headline number.

Down in Virginia's southeastern corner, Norfolk occupies the spot where the Elizabeth River empties toward the Chesapeake Bay. Neighborhoods and how they differ

Dozens of named neighborhoods make up the city, and a house on one street can have little in common with a house two miles away.

  • Freemason and West Freemason: historic downtown blocks holding some of Norfolk's oldest buildings.
  • Berkley: once a separate city, annexed in 1906, across the Elizabeth River.
  • Willoughby Spit and Ocean View: bay-front areas.

Flood zones and the Forerunner tool

The city is low, mostly ringed by water and slowly sinking, and some areas already flood at high tide. Tropical storm risk is highest from mid-August through September, when heavy rain and wind can hit.

Zones come from FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map. Norfolk applies them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance together with the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The Flood Zones page on the city's site describes each one.

Hooff's Run carries water from parts of Northridge, Del Ray and Rosemont, so owners there hear about drainage often.

As a Class 6 community in the National Flood Insurance Program's Community Rating System, Alexandria can offer residents a discount of up to 20 percent on flood insurance premiums. A flood mitigation grant program and help with sewer backflow prevention are also available. See the city's flooding and drainage page.

On the state disclosure form the owner makes no claim about special flood hazard areas, and buyers are sent to FEMA maps. Even so, expect questions if your basement ever took in water, and answer in writing.

Blacksburg in brief

Blacksburg is an incorporated town in Montgomery County, in the New River Valley of southwest Virginia. It is the largest town in the state, with 44,826 residents in 2020. Because it is a town and not an independent city, county offices and town offices both play a part in property matters. Virginia Tech dominates the local economy and the housing market, so the market here behaves differently from most Virginia towns of its size.

Blacksburg is about 10 miles north of Christiansburg and the I-81 interchange, and the drive to Roanoke usually takes less than an hour.

Old houses and new ones

William Black laid out a 16-block grid in 1797, and the town was incorporated in 1871. Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, now Virginia Tech, opened in 1872. Growth stayed modest for most of the next century: 3,358 people in 1950 and 9,384 in 1970. Then Virginia Tech was annexed into the town and the count jumped to 30,638 by 1980. The Hethwood development grew in the 1970s.

Houses near Main Street and College Avenue sit on the oldest part of the town plan. A house's age tells you a lot about which systems are original, which is why we ask for the build year and roof age at the start of every conversation.

Selling near Virginia Tech

The buyer pool, the rental pool and the calendar are all tied to the university. The median age was 21.7 in 2020, and only 24.7 percent of households were married couples. About 30.9 percent were people living alone. A large share of local demand is for rentals, shared houses and small units rather than family homes.

  • Rental houses: a house leased to students on a yearly cycle is easiest to sell when you can document the lease end date and show a clean walkthrough.
  • Owner-occupied houses: faculty, staff and research employees often buy near campus and the Virginia Tech Corporate Research Center.
  • Timing: a vacant house in July is easier to show than an occupied one in May during finals.

Is your house easy to reach on foot or by bus?

Blacksburg Transit runs mostly to and from the Virginia Tech campus, and every passenger rides free. A regional commuter route called the Smart Way Bus connects Virginia Tech, downtown Blacksburg, Christiansburg, the Roanoke-Blacksburg Regional Airport and Roanoke. The Huckleberry Trail, built on the old railbed, runs through town and is a selling point for houses nearby.

Walkability to campus, a bus stop or the downtown core generally matters more to Blacksburg buyers than a big yard. If your house sits close to a bus line, put that in your listing or offer request. A house on a long drive outside the core will be judged on commute time.

Winter and the house itself

At this elevation Blacksburg gets about 24.7 inches of snow in a typical season, from December through March, and about 42.6 inches of precipitation a year. The practical effect on a house is roof load and heating cost. After a snowstorm dropped about two feet in February 2010, the gym roof of the former Blacksburg High School collapsed. Most houses are built to local snow load standards, but flat or low-slope roofs on older additions are worth having checked.

  • Inspect the framing under roofs on porches and rear additions before you list.
  • Confirm that the furnace or heat pump runs in the cold months, not only in the fall.
  • Check that gutters and downspouts carry water away from foundations.

Winter weather also affects showing schedules, and a house that is easy to walk on a snowy day sells better.

Town services and who bills what

Montgomery County Public Schools runs the public schools in Blacksburg, not the town. The town government has a council and a mayor. Ask the town's planning and building staff before you rent the house, change its use or plan an addition. For real estate tax bills, ask the town and Montgomery County offices which of them bills your parcel.

What a seller owes at settlement

A grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500 of price falls on the seller by default, though the contract may shift part or all of it to the buyer. The money is split between the state and the locality, and the circuit court clerk holds the deed until it is paid.

Real estate tax still owed ranks ahead of every other lien, so the closing agent takes it out of your proceeds. The contract splits the current year between you and the buyer. The buyer also gets the Virginia Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement, in which you make no statement about historic district rules, flood hazard areas, wastewater systems such as septic tanks, radon, or nearness to a public use airport. It tells the buyer to investigate.

The septic line matters if the house is not on public sewer. With a septic system, have pumping and repair records ready, and add a note about where the tank and drain field sit if you know. The statutes are Virginia Code 58.1-802, 58.1-3340 and 55.1-703.

Before you contact a buyer

Pull together a short file: the lease and deposit details if the house is rented, the build year and roof age, any septic records, and a list of repairs you already know about. Walk through the house with a phone camera and note anything a buyer would find on day one. Being open about problems early shortens the conversation, and it makes a written offer easier to trust. If you owe money on the house, ask the lender for a payoff letter so the numbers are in hand before closing is scheduled.

Selling quickly for cash

With no buyer financing or appraisal to wait on, a cash sale often lets you choose a closing date that suits your move or your tenants' lease. Give us the address and a few facts about the house, and we will review it and send a written offer. You are free to decline.

A few situations come up again and again: an investor ready to leave a student rental, a family with an inherited house, an owner moving for work, or a house with deferred maintenance that is hard to show during the school year. We buy as is, so painting, patching and clearing out are not required before closing.

Is Blacksburg a city or a town?

It is a town in Montgomery County, not an independent city. It is Virginia's largest town by population, so county offices and town offices both play a role in property matters.

Yes. You can sell a rental with tenants in place and the buyer takes over the lease terms, or you can set the closing for after the lease ends. Share the lease and deposit details early.

About 24.7 inches in a typical season, mostly from December through March. Have older flat or low-slope roofs checked before you list.

Who pays the Virginia grantor's tax in a Blacksburg sale?

The seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise. The rate is 50 cents per $500 of the sale price under Virginia Code 58.1-802.

On the state form the owner makes no claim about a wastewater system's type, size or upkeep, and buyers are urged to check. Keep pumping and repair records handy, since inspectors and buyers ask.

City or county: check which one you are in

Charlottesville is an independent city in central Virginia and the county seat of Albemarle County. A house with a Charlottesville mailing address can sit in the county, and most of the University of Virginia's grounds are legally in Albemarle County even though they feel like part of town.

That line decides who assesses your property, who issues permits and which zoning rules apply. Look at your tax bill first. The name at the top tells you which government you deal with, and it is worth settling before you talk to any buyer or agent.

Older core and newer subdivisions

When you contact us, the first thing we ask for is the year the house was built. A century-old house may have plaster walls, original wiring and a stone or brick foundation.   • Later subdivisions: check roof age, HVAC age and water around the foundation.

Who buys and rents in Charlottesville

The University of Virginia and its health system anchor the job base, along with city government and the city school board, each at more than 1,000 employees. Only about 18 percent of people employed in the city live in it. About 82 percent commute in, and 42 percent of those commuters come from Albemarle County, while 11,497 city residents commute out.

Weather and what it does to a house

Summers are hot and humid, winters are cool, and it rains in every month. July averages about 77.6 degrees and January about 36.2. The high passes 90 degrees on roughly 34 days a year, and snow averages 17 inches a season but rarely stays long. The wettest stretch runs from May through September.

  • Inspect the attic and the roof.
  • Look at the ground around the foundation for erosion or pooling after storms.

Location and transit

Interstate 64 and U.S. 29 are the main highways, with U.S. 250 and Route 20 also serving the city. I-64 runs east toward Richmond and west toward Staunton, and U.S. 29 runs northeast toward the Washington area and southwest toward Lynchburg. Charlottesville Area Transit runs city buses, JAUNT runs paratransit vans, and University Transit Service covers the campus area. The Amtrak station is served by the Cardinal three times a week, plus daily Crescent and Northeast Regional trains.

A house within walking distance of the Downtown Mall or a bus corridor appeals to renters and downsizers. A house outside the core appeals to buyers who drive. We weigh both when we put together a cash offer.

Charlottesville City Schools run six elementary schools, Walker Upper Elementary School, Buford Middle School and Charlottesville High School. Albemarle County Public Schools serve the surrounding county. If you are unsure which government covers your house, the school division on your child's records is one more clue, though some private schools with a Charlottesville postal address are actually in the county.

Part goes to the state and part to the locality, and Albemarle's circuit court clerk holds the deed until the money arrives. The rule is Virginia Code 58.1-802.

A tax bill left unpaid becomes a lien ranking above most others. At the settlement table, the closing agent clears it from what you would otherwise take home, and the contract decides how the current year's bill is split between you and the buyer. See Virginia Code 58.1-3340.

Sellers also hand over the Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement. On that form the owner declines to make any representation about historic district rules, lot lines, neighboring parcels, flood hazards, easements, lead plumbing, drywall or a dam's condition. From January 1, 2027, the statute adds a line about use-value assessment and roll-back taxes. Read Virginia Code 55.1-703 for the wording.

People in town tend to call us about a parent's house after probate, a rental with a worn-out kitchen, or a job transfer that leaves little time. Snowfall averages about 17 inches a season, though it changes a lot year to year and rarely lingers. Summer is hot and humid, with about 34 days a year above 90 degrees.

Selling a house in Manassas

Manassas is a self-governing city that serves as the seat of Prince William County. Right beside it lies another independent city, Manassas Park. Residents numbered 42,772 in the 2020 census, and the 2025 estimate is 44,332. Statistically it belongs to the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria metro area.

That independence shapes your paperwork. Your assessment and your tax bill come from two city offices, the Commissioner of the Revenue and the Treasurer. Nothing goes through a county office.

Homes here rarely sit empty. In 2020 the city had 13,983 households sharing 14,365 housing units, and just 2.7% of those units were vacant. Homeowner vacancy ran 0.7 percent and rental vacancy 3.3 percent.

Older 1980s housing and what buyers check

Around Old Town the housing is old, and across the rest of the city a big slice dates to the 1980s. About 35 percent of the stock was built from 1980 to 1989, which was the fastest stretch of growth the city has seen.

Houses from that decade are now about 40 years old. Roofs, furnaces, air conditioners and water heaters could be at or past their expected life. An inspector hired by a buyer will check each one first. In a traditional sale that often leads to a repair request. A buyer who purchases as is folds the condition into the offer instead, so you can skip the contractors.

Commuting from Manassas

Plenty of residents earn their paychecks elsewhere. Around 16,700 head out to jobs in nearby areas, with many going to Fairfax and Prince William counties. The average trip takes about 34.7 minutes. About 73 percent drive alone and 4 percent ride transit.

Virginia Routes 28, 234 and 234 Business cross the city, while I-66 and US 29 pass nearby. Trains stop at the Manassas station, which Virginia Railway Express and Amtrak share with the city's visitor center. If your house is close to the station or a main road, say so when you talk to a buyer.

How Manassas bills real estate tax

Two installments a year, December 5 and June 5, make up the real estate tax calendar. The city's fiscal year opens July 1. Escrow accounts and missed bills

With an escrow account, your mortgage company typically sends the tax payment itself, and the Treasurer skips mailing the homeowner a copy. Should one show up in your mailbox anyway, hand it to your lender right away.

Some past-due accounts get sent to a collection firm. Virginia law is clear that a bill you never received still carries penalty and interest, so check with the Treasurer that nothing is overdue. The collection line is 703-257-8241, and City Hall sits at 9027 Center Street.

Tax relief for older and disabled owners

Tax Relief is the city program for owners aged 65 or older and for some owners with disabilities, offering an exemption or a deferral. Living in the house and think you qualify? Ask the city before you list. A deferral taken in an earlier year can leave an amount that must be paid off when the house changes hands.

What happens at closing

You sign the deed and a settlement statement. The statement shows what is subtracted from the price: a loan payoff if there is one, real estate tax still owed, and the state's deed charges. The remainder goes to you.

Virginia's grantor tax works out to 50 cents per $500 of value, and the sales contract decides who owes it. When the contract is silent, the seller pays. The clerk also insists that page one of the deed state the price before it is recorded. Your settlement agent totals everything, and the city can explain any local rule that affects your lot.

Documents to gather, and steps a cash buyer skips

Lay out a photo ID, your deed if you can find it, mortgage account details and the newest city tax bill. Landlords should add the lease. Heirs should collect whatever shows who may sign for the estate.

With a cash buyer there is no lender appraisal, no waiting on a loan approval, and no chance that financing collapses days before closing. The repair list that tends to follow a buyer's inspection is also avoided. Taxes and liens still have to be cleared, but they come out of your proceeds, so you do not pay them beforehand.

Timing a sale around the tax calendar

Because installments land in early December and early June, a closing close to either date is worth planning. Ask the Treasurer whether the coming installment has been billed and whether your account shows a balance. If it has not been paid, the settlement agent will usually subtract it from your check, and the buyer's side will want to see that it is settled.

A cash sale can close as quickly as the title search allows, so you are able to line up the closing with the day you hand over the house instead of working around a lender's calendar. Share your move date at the start and the buyer can build the schedule around it.

Questions to ask any cash buyer

Ask who is paying for the title search and the settlement company, who covers the grantor tax, and whether the offer assumes you will leave the house empty or as it stands. Get the closing date in writing. Find out whether the buyer needs access for a walk-through beforehand. A fair buyer answers each of these plainly and does not push you to sign before you have talked to the Treasurer about your balance.

Situations Manassas sellers often face

  • Rentals with tenants in place or repairs put off for years.

  • Tax and escrow loose ends that need to be tied up before closing.

Selling directly means you choose the closing date and leave the house as it is. There are no open houses and no punch list.

When are Manassas real estate taxes due?

Taxes are due in two installments, on December 5 and June 5. The fiscal year starts July 1.

Who assesses property in Manassas?

The Commissioner of the Revenue sets assessments for real property. The Treasurer then bills and collects the tax.

I have an escrow account. Who pays my Manassas tax bill?

Your mortgage company normally pays it. If a bill reaches you anyway, send it to your lender, since the Treasurer's office does not mail copies to homeowners.

Do I pay a transfer tax when I sell a Manassas house?

Getting an older Salem house ready to show

Even if you plan to sell as is, a few inexpensive steps help any buyer see the house clearly. Clear the walkways, open the blinds and make sure the utilities are on for the visit. Gather what you know about the roof, the heating and cooling system and the plumbing, since buyers in older neighborhoods ask about those first. If you would rather not do any of it, a cash buyer takes the house as it stands.

Cash sale or listing?

Listing in the traditional way means getting the house ready, hosting showings, haggling over repairs after the inspection and waiting for the buyer's lender. A cash sale avoids the lender and usually the haggling.

  • A listing fits a house in good shape when you are willing to wait for the best price.
  • Selling by owner saves the agent's commission, though marketing and paperwork fall to you.
  • A cash offer fits inherited, tenant-occupied, damaged or behind-on-payments houses, where speed and certainty outrank top dollar.

Whichever way you go, compare the amount that would reach you after taxes, repairs and carrying costs.

Frequently asked questions

Is Salem, Virginia part of Roanoke County?

No. Salem is an independent city and a separate jurisdiction, though it is the county seat of Roanoke County. It has its own courthouse and sheriff's office, and the county's administrative offices are in Cave Spring.

Who pays the deed taxes when a house sells in Salem?

The seller normally pays the grantor's tax of 50 cents per $500, and the state recordation tax of 25 cents per $100 is charged on the deed. The buyer and seller can agree to shift the grantor's tax. Your closing statement shows the exact amounts.

Can I sell an inherited house in Salem without a listing?

Yes, as long as the person signing has legal authority to sell, such as an executor or a named heir after the estate is settled. Confirm with the estate's attorney before you accept any offer.

How fast can a cash sale close in Salem?

Timing depends on title work, liens, probate status and when you want to move. A cash buyer does not wait on a mortgage underwriter, so the title search often sets the date.

Where do I find Salem's current property tax due dates?

Ask the City of Salem Treasurer or Commissioner of the Revenue.

A town inside Fairfax County

Herndon is an incorporated town in Fairfax County, in the Washington, D.C. metro area of Northern Virginia, and the largest of the county's three incorporated towns. It covers 4.29 square miles at about 361 feet of elevation, and 24,655 people lived here at the 2020 census. A little over two acres of the town technically lie in Loudoun County.

Because a Virginia town sits within a county, Herndon owners deal with two governments. The town runs its own council and police department, while Fairfax County handles assessment and tax billing. Housing was tight in 2020, with 8,133 units and only 2.9 percent vacant, so a house that sits unsold for a long time tends to stand out.

How the town grew

The settlement took the name Herndon in 1858, after a naval officer who died with his ship while helping save more than 150 passengers and crew. It grew as a dairy and vacation hub along the Alexandria, Loudoun and Hampshire Railroad, later the Washington and Old Dominion Railroad. The old rail line is now the W&OD trail, the depot is a museum, and the Herndon Historic District is on the National Register of Historic Places.

Most growth came late: 1,960 people in 1960, 11,449 in 1980 and 24,655 in 2020. That means most houses date from the later twentieth century, with older ones near the historic downtown.

Technology jobs and the buyer pool

Herndon belongs to the Dulles Technology Corridor, and its largest employers are technology and government contractors. Serco has 500 to 749 employees, and Amazon Web Services, Karsun Solutions, Northwest Federal Credit Union, Peraton and Boeing each have 250 to 499.

The buyer pool therefore includes contractors and government workers whose plans can swing with a job change or a security clearance timeline. Sellers in the same field sometimes have to close quickly when a relocation arrives.

Roads, Metro and parks

State Route 228 crosses the center of town along Elden Street, Monroe Street, Park Avenue and Dranesville Road, and a truck route follows Herndon Parkway around downtown. At the south end, Route 228 meets State Route 267, the Dulles Toll Road, which leads to Washington by way of Interstate 66 and to Dulles International Airport.

The Silver Line extension opened in 2022 with a Herndon station. A house within walking or short driving distance can draw different buyers than one on a cul-de-sac farther away, though the effect on any single sale varies. Every residence is within a mile of a public park, and the town has a community center, an aquatic center and the Herndon Centennial Golf Course.

Schools

Herndon is part of the Fairfax County Public Schools district. Clearview, Dranesville, Herndon and Hutchison elementary schools, Herndon Middle School and Herndon High School serve students inside the town limits. Zoning can change, so confirm boundaries with the district for a specific address.

Real estate tax: who bills and when

Fairfax County collects Herndon's town tax, and it appears on the county real estate bill. The town's Fiscal Year 2027 rate is $0.27 per $100 of assessed value. The county sets its own rate separately, so use the county's tax pages to see the full bill.

With installments in July and December, a closing near either date should settle who pays the bill that is due, and your title company can prorate it.

Why Herndon owners sell

In a high-cost commuter town, the same few situations come up.

  • An owner who bought years ago, now lives out of the area and holds a house that needs updating.
  • An inherited house shared among several heirs who disagree on timing.
  • A rental that has been through several tenants.
  • Deferred repairs that make a bank appraisal or a buyer's inspection risky.

Rules for historic properties, permits and rentals come from the town and the county, so ask both before you renovate or rent.

How a cash sale works in Herndon

A cash sale means the buyer needs no mortgage. You describe the house and receive a written offer. If you accept, the title or settlement company handles liens, tax proration and recording, and closing can be arranged around your date.

An as-is sale is often the simplest way out of a house that would need major work. Compare it with the cost of repairs, agent fees and months of mortgage, tax and utility payments on a listing. The net figure matters more than the headline price.

Have the deed, your loan payoff information and, for a shared inheritance, agreement among the heirs on who signs. A title company will tell you what else it needs once it opens the file.

When several heirs share a house

Shared inheritances stall more Herndon sales than any repair does. One heir wants to wait for a better market, another needs cash now, and a third lives across the country. Nobody can sign a deed alone until the estate paperwork names who has authority.

  • Settle who holds authority to sign before you ask for an offer.
  • Agree on a price range and a closing window as a group, in writing if you can.
  • Decide who handles the walk-through and who receives the proceeds.
  • Tell the title company early if an heir will sign from another state.

A cash buyer can work around a family's timetable, because there is no lender's deadline. Even so, the sale only moves as fast as the slowest signature, so bring everyone into the conversation before an offer arrives.

Listing versus selling for cash

A traditional listing may bring a higher price when the house is updated and you can wait. It also brings showings, a buyer's inspection and a loan appraisal, and any of them can reopen the price.

Selling for cash skips those steps. The trade is a lower price in return for speed and a closing day you can count on. To compare honestly, estimate repairs, agent fees and the months of mortgage, tax and utility payments a listing would cost, subtract them from the listing price and set the result next to the cash offer.

Paperwork to gather

Pull these together before you ask anyone for an offer, and the title work will go faster.

  • The deed and your most recent Fairfax County real estate bill.
  • A loan payoff statement from your lender, if a mortgage remains.
  • The name of anyone else on the title.
  • Any town or county permits for past work on the house.
  • Photos of the roof, kitchen, bathrooms and the heating and cooling system.

Permits matter in an older house. If a deck, basement or addition was built without one, tell the buyer early, because the title company and any later inspector may notice.

Is Herndon a town or a city?

When are Herndon real estate taxes due?

The first installment is due July 28 and the second is due December 5. Delinquent balances are subject to penalties and interest.

Which school district serves Herndon?
